issues.legal_issue: The extended limitation period for possession of a hereditary office applies only when the defendant possesses the office adversely to the claimant.
material_facts: The claimants sought declarations and an injunction based on alleged hereditary rights to serve as worshippers, together with accounts.
The defendants were trustees who had dismissed the claimants’ predecessors and appointed other servants to perform the worship.
The trustees neither performed the duties of the hereditary office themselves nor received its profits, and the replacement servants did not claim to hold the office hereditarily.
issues.conclusion: The suits were governed by the residuary limitation article, not the article governing possession of a hereditary office.
issues.legal_principle: Article 124 of the Limitation Act, 1908, requires a claim for possession of a hereditary office against a defendant who has taken possession of that office adversely to the plaintiff; its third column cannot be ignored when determining its application. The Court approved Thathachariar v. Singarachariar, referred to Jhalandar Thakur v. Jharula Das, and held Kunj Bihari Prasadji v. Keshavlal Hiralal and Jalim Singh Srimal v. Choonee Lall Johurry inapplicable and Annasami v. Adivarachari distinguishable.

rule.if: hereditary_service_rights_suit and claimants_asserted_hereditary_office and trustees_appointed_replacement_servants and trustees_neither_performed_office_nor_received_office_profits

predicates.hereditary_service_rights_suit: The proceeding seeks relief based on a claimed hereditary right to perform services attached to an office.
predicates.claimants_asserted_hereditary_office: The claimants asserted that they held the office hereditarily.
predicates.trustees_appointed_replacement_servants: The trustees appointed other people to perform the office’s duties as servants of the institution.
predicates.trustees_neither_performed_office_nor_re: The trustees did not themselves perform the office’s duties or receive its profits.

issues.definition: When claimants assert hereditary rights in a service proceeding, but trustees appoint replacement servants and neither perform the office nor receive its profits, the adverse-possession limitation rule for hereditary offices does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for hereditary service rights accrues when those rights are clearly and effectively denied, and a suit filed beyond the applicable limitation period is barred.
material_facts: The claimants’ earlier claim of ownership had been rejected, while their alleged lesser rights as hereditary worshippers remained unresolved.
The trustees’ 1922 possession suit expressly denied the claimants’ rights as hereditary servants, and the claimants asserted those rights in response.
A decree for the trustees followed, and the claimants were dispossessed in execution of it.
The present suits were filed more than six years after the denial and decree.
issues.conclusion: The right to sue accrued no later than the decree and resulting dispossession, and the suits were barred by limitation under the residuary limitation article.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation begins when the right to sue accrues. The Court held that the clear denial of the hereditary rights, confirmed by the decree and dispossession, gave rise to the cause of action; the suits filed more than six years later were out of time.

rule.if: hereditary_service_rights_suit and defendants_clearly_denied_claimants_rights and denial_was_confirmed_by_decree_or_ousting and claim_filed_long_after_clear_denial

predicates.hereditary_service_rights_suit: The proceeding seeks relief based on a claimed hereditary right to perform services attached to an office.
predicates.defendants_clearly_denied_claimants_righ: The defendants expressly and unequivocally denied the claimants’ asserted rights.
predicates.denial_was_confirmed_by_decree_or_oustin: A decree or resulting ouster confirmed the denial of the asserted rights.
predicates.claim_filed_long_after_clear_denial: The claimants filed suit long after their rights had been clearly denied.

issues.definition: A hereditary-service claim is barred when the defendants clearly deny the rights, that denial is confirmed by a decree or ousting, and the claimants sue long afterward.

issues.legal_issue: A completed ouster is not a continuing wrong merely because the resulting dispossession continues.
material_facts: The trustees obtained a decree for possession and dispossessed the claimants in execution of it.
The claimants’ injury to their asserted rights was complete when the ouster occurred.
The claimants remained dispossessed, but there was no recurring wrongful act by the trustees after the ouster.
issues.conclusion: Section 23 of the Limitation Act, 1908, did not apply to extend limitation because the injury was complete at the ouster and only its effects continued.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Limitation Act, 1908, concerns a continuing wrong: an act that creates a continuing source of injury and makes the actor liable for its continuance. Continuing damage from a completed injury is not itself a continuing wrong. The Court distinguished Maharani Rajroop Koer v. Syed Abdul Hossein and Hukum Chand v. Maharaj Bahadur Singh, and referred to Choudhury Bibhuti Narayan Singh v. Maharaja Sir Guru Mahadev Asram Prasad Sahi Bahadur and Khair Mohammad Khan v. Mst. Jannat.

rule.if: hereditary_service_rights_suit and defendants_caused_ousting and injury_completed_at_ousting and only_dispossession_effects_continued

predicates.hereditary_service_rights_suit: The proceeding seeks relief based on a claimed hereditary right to perform services attached to an office.
predicates.defendants_caused_ousting: The defendants caused the claimants to be excluded from the office or its performance.
predicates.injury_completed_at_ousting: The injury to the asserted right was complete when the claimants were ousted.
predicates.only_dispossession_effects_continued: After the ouster, the continuing condition was the effect of dispossession rather than a recurring wrongful act.

issues.definition: When an ouster completes the injury and only its effects persist, the continuing-wrong rule does not extend limitation.
